ppl.sargon.t: First to unite the cities of Sumer and Akkad; the Akkadian Empire is founded in the late twenty-fourth century BC. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.ramesses-ii.t: Pharaoh of the 19th Dynasty who fought the Hittites and built on a colossal scale. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.sappho.t: Lyric poet of Lesbos whose songs survive only in fragments; born about 630 BC.
ppl.nebuchadnezzar-ii.t: King of Babylon who rebuilt his capital and carried off the Judaeans. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.mahavira.t: The twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of Jainism.
ppl.mahavira.works.0.t: Jain Agamas (oral teachings compiled by the ganadharas)
ppl.pythagoras.t: Taught number and harmony at Croton in southern Italy; dates are approximate.
ppl.buddha.t: Taught in the Ganges plain; the traditional dates are c. 563–483 BC, and some scholars put his death nearer 400 BC.
ppl.buddha.works.0.t: Pali Canon (written down in Sri Lanka)
ppl.cyrus.t: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire, who took Babylon in 539 BC. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.confucius.t: Teacher of Lu whose sayings shaped Chinese thought for two millennia.
ppl.confucius.works.0.t: Analects (compiled by disciples after his death)
ppl.sun-tzu.t: Attributed author of The Art of War; dates are approximate.
ppl.heraclitus.t: Philosopher of flux at Ephesus; dates are approximate.
ppl.darius.t: Organised the Persian empire into satrapies and began Persepolis. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.xerxes.t: Led the invasion of Greece in 480 BC that ended at Salamis. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.socrates.t: Questioned Athens in its streets and was put to death in 399 BC.
ppl.mozi.t: Founder of Mohism, preaching impartial care; dates are approximate.
ppl.aristotle.t: Tutor to Alexander; taught at the Lyceum in Athens.
ppl.mencius.t: Confucian thinker of the Warring States; dates most accepted are 372–289 BC.
ppl.chanakya.t: Minister of Chandragupta Maurya and traditional author of the Arthashastra; dates are approximate.
ppl.epicurus.t: Taught in his Garden at Athens.
ppl.alexander.t: King of Macedon who conquered the Persian empire and died at Babylon in June 323 BC. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.zeno-of-citium.t: Founder of the Stoa at Athens.
ppl.xunzi.t: Confucian who held human nature to be shaped by ritual and learning.
ppl.archimedes.t: Mathematician and engineer of Syracuse, known for his principle of buoyancy and his screw; dates are approximate.
ppl.ashoka.t: Mauryan emperor who, after the Kalinga war, sent Buddhist missions abroad. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.qin-shi-huang.t: First emperor of a united China from 221 BC; buried at Mount Li with the terracotta army.
ppl.dong-zhongshu.t: Han scholar who made Confucianism the learning of the state; dates are approximate.
ppl.dong-zhongshu.works.0.t: Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals
ppl.pompey.t: Roman general and rival of Caesar, killed in Egypt in 48 BC.
ppl.cicero.t: Orator and philosopher of the late Republic.
ppl.caesar.t: Conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC and was killed on 15 March 44 BC.
ppl.lucretius.t: Epicurean poet of On the Nature of Things.
ppl.horace.t: Roman lyric poet of the Augustan age.
ppl.augustus.t: First Roman emperor, victor at Actium in 31 BC and Augustus from 27 BC.
ppl.ovid.t: Poet of the Metamorphoses, exiled to the Black Sea.
ppl.jesus.t: Teacher from Galilee whose followers founded Christianity; the timeline dates his life c. 6–4 BC to AD 30 or 33.
ppl.seneca.t: Stoic philosopher and tutor of Nero.
ppl.wang-chong.t: Han sceptic and author of the Lunheng.
ppl.epictetus.t: Former slave who taught Stoicism at Nicopolis; dates are approximate.
ppl.marcus-aurelius.t: Emperor and Stoic author of the Meditations.
ppl.nagarjuna.t: Buddhist philosopher of the Middle Way; dates are approximate.
ppl.nagarjuna.works.0.t: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (Root Verses on the Middle Way)
ppl.plotinus.t: Founder of Neoplatonism, teaching at Rome.
ppl.constantine.t: Emperor who granted toleration at Milan in 313 and founded Constantinople in 330. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.augustine.t: Bishop of Hippo and author of the Confessions and the City of God.
ppl.boethius.t: Wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison under Theoderic.
ppl.justinian.t: Codified Roman law, built Hagia Sophia and reconquered Africa and Italy. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.muhammad.t: Prophet of Islam, who left Mecca for Medina in 622; born about 570.
ppl.li-bai.t: Tang poet of wine, moonlight and wandering.
ppl.du-fu.t: Tang poet whose verse recorded the An Lushan rebellion.
ppl.shankara.t: Teacher of Advaita Vedanta; dates are approximate.
ppl.al-kindi.t: First philosopher of the Arabs, at the Abbasid court; born about 801.
ppl.alfred.t: King of the Anglo-Saxons who held Wessex against the Danes; born about 849.
ppl.al-farabi.t: The Second Teacher after Aristotle; born about 870.
ppl.ferdowsi.t: Author of the Shahnameh, the Persian book of kings.
ppl.vladimir.t: Prince of Novgorod and grand prince of Kiev who had the Rus' baptised in 988. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.murasaki.t: Lady of the Heian court and author of The Tale of Genji; born about 973, died perhaps 1014.
ppl.avicenna.t: Physician and philosopher whose Canon of Medicine was read for six centuries; born about 980.
ppl.omar-khayyam.t: Mathematician, astronomer and poet of the quatrains.
ppl.omar-khayyam.works.1.t: Commentary on the Postulates of Euclid
ppl.al-ghazali.t: Jurist, theologian and Sufi of Tus; his Incoherence of the Philosophers answered Avicenna, and after a crisis in 1095 he left Baghdad to write the Revival of the Religious Sciences. Born c. 1058 and died in Tus on 19 December 1111.
ppl.al-ghazali.works.1.t: The Revival of the Religious Sciences
ppl.hildegard.t: Abbess, visionary and composer of plainchant.
ppl.averroes.t: The Commentator on Aristotle, judge at Córdoba; born about 1126.
ppl.zhu-xi.t: Synthesiser of Neo-Confucianism, whose commentaries became the examination canon.
ppl.zhu-xi.works.1.t: Collected Commentaries on the Four Books
ppl.maimonides.t: Rabbi, physician and author of the Guide for the Perplexed; born about 1135.
ppl.genghis-khan.t: Proclaimed khan of all the Mongols in 1206; invaded the Jin in 1211 and Khwarazm in 1219; born about 1162.
ppl.saadi.t: Persian poet of the Gulistan and the Bustan.
ppl.rumi.t: Persian poet and Sufi mystic of Konya.
ppl.aquinas.t: Dominican author of the Summa Theologiae; born about 1221.
ppl.dante.t: Florentine poet of the Divine Comedy, who died in exile at Ravenna.
ppl.ockham.t: Franciscan logician and nominalist, born c. 1287 at Ockham in Surrey; summoned to Avignon, he fled to the court of Louis of Bavaria in 1328 and died in Munich, probably in April 1347.
ppl.petrarch.t: Scholar and poet of the Canzoniere, the first humanist.
ppl.hafez.works.0.t: Divan of Hafez (compiled after his death)
ppl.ibn-khaldun.t: Historian of Tunis, born 27 May 1332, whose Muqaddimah, written in six months before 1378, set out a theory of the rise and fall of dynasties; he died in Cairo on 17 March 1406.
ppl.chaucer.t: Author of the Canterbury Tales; born about 1343.
ppl.gutenberg.t: Printer of Mainz who introduced movable-type printing to Europe.
ppl.sejong.t: King of Joseon under whom the Korean alphabet was created. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.kabir.t: Mystic poet of Varanasi revered by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs.
ppl.kabir.works.0.t: Bijak (written down in the seventeenth century)
ppl.ivan-iii.t: Grand prince of Moscow who gathered the Russian lands and faced down the Horde on the Ugra in 1480. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.erasmus.t: Humanist of Rotterdam, editor of the Greek New Testament.
ppl.machiavelli.t: Florentine secretary and author of The Prince.
ppl.wang-yangming.t: Ming philosopher of the unity of knowledge and action.
ppl.copernicus.t: Canon of Frombork whose De revolutionibus of 1543 put the sun at the centre.
ppl.thomas-more.t: Author of Utopia, executed under Henry VIII.
ppl.luther.t: Posted the Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg in 1517.
ppl.luther.works.1.t: To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation
ppl.suleiman.t: Sultan from 1520 who took Belgrade and Rhodes, won at Mohács and besieged Vienna in 1529.
ppl.montaigne.t: Inventor of the essay, writing in his tower near Bordeaux.
ppl.cervantes.t: Author of Don Quixote, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615.
ppl.akbar.t: Mughal emperor who widened the empire and held debates between faiths. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.elizabeth-i.t: Protestant queen of England and first Supreme Governor of its church. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.francis-bacon.t: Lord Chancellor and advocate of experimental method.
ppl.shakespeare.t: Poet and playwright of the Globe; died in 1616.
ppl.galileo.t: Turned the telescope on Jupiter's moons in 1610 and was tried at Rome in 1633.
ppl.galileo.works.2.t: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems
ppl.monteverdi.t: Composer of Orfeo and the Vespers, master of music at St Mark's.
ppl.kepler.t: Found the elliptical orbits of the planets at Prague.
ppl.descartes.t: Wrote the Discourse on Method in the Dutch Republic.
ppl.milton.t: Poet of Paradise Lost and defender of the Commonwealth.
ppl.gustavus-adolphus.t: King of Sweden who entered the Thirty Years' War and fell at Lützen. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.pascal.t: Mathematician, physicist and author of the Pensées.
ppl.spinoza.t: Lens-grinder and author of the Ethics.
ppl.locke.t: Author of the Two Treatises and the Essay on Human Understanding.
ppl.louis-xiv.t: The Sun King, who moved his court to Versailles. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.newton.t: Published the Principia in 1687; born 1642 in the old calendar.
ppl.basho.t: Master of the haiku and of the travel sketch.
ppl.basho.works.3.t: Oku no Hosomichi (The Narrow Road to the Deep North)
ppl.leibniz.t: Philosopher and mathematician, co-inventor of the calculus.
ppl.vico.t: Neapolitan philosopher of history, born 23 June 1668, whose New Science of 1725 read the course of nations in their myths and languages; he died in Naples on 23 January 1744.
ppl.vico.works.0.t: On the Study Methods of Our Time
ppl.vico.works.1.t: On the Most Ancient Wisdom of the Italians
ppl.peter-the-great.t: Tsar who travelled west in 1697–1698, founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 and won at Poltava in 1709.
ppl.handel.t: Composer of opera and oratorio in London.
ppl.berkeley.t: Irish philosopher and bishop of Cloyne, born 12 March 1685 at Dysart Castle near Thomastown; his Principles of 1710 argued that to be is to be perceived. He died in Oxford on 14 January 1753.
ppl.berkeley.works.0.t: An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision
ppl.berkeley.works.1.t: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
ppl.berkeley.works.2.t: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous
ppl.montesquieu.t: Author of The Spirit of the Laws.
ppl.montesquieu.works.1.t: Considerations on the Causes of the Greatness of the Romans and their Decline
ppl.voltaire.t: Philosopher of the Enlightenment, at Paris and Ferney.
ppl.lomonosov.t: Polymath of the Petersburg academy and reformer of the Russian language.
ppl.lomonosov.works.0.t: Ode on the Taking of Khotin
ppl.lomonosov.works.1.t: Letter on the Rules of Russian Versification
ppl.hume.t: Sceptical philosopher and historian of Edinburgh.
ppl.hume.works.2.t: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
ppl.rousseau.t: Genevan author of The Social Contract and Émile.
ppl.adam-smith.t: Author of The Wealth of Nations.
ppl.kant.t: Never left Königsberg; the Critique of Pure Reason appeared in 1781.
ppl.kant.works.1.t: Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals
ppl.cook.t: Charted the Pacific on three voyages from 1768.
ppl.haydn.t: Composer of the Esterházy court and of Vienna.
ppl.goethe.t: Poet of Faust, minister at Weimar.
ppl.mozart.t: Composer of Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute.
ppl.schiller.t: Poet and playwright, Goethe's friend at Weimar.
ppl.catherine-ii.t: Empress of Russia who bought the pictures that founded the Hermitage. The years given are those of the reign.
ppl.napoleon.t: Born 15 August 1769; emperor from 1804; died on St Helena on 5 May 1821.
ppl.beethoven.t: Composer of nine symphonies, in Vienna from 1792.
ppl.hegel.t: Philosopher of history and the dialectic, at Berlin from 1818.
ppl.hegel.works.3.t: Elements of the Philosophy of Right
ppl.wordsworth.t: Romantic poet of the Lake District.
ppl.gauss.t: The prince of mathematicians, at Göttingen.
ppl.schopenhauer.t: Author of The World as Will and Representation.
ppl.schopenhauer.works.0.t: On the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason
ppl.schopenhauer.works.1.t: The World as Will and Representation
ppl.faraday.t: Discoverer of electromagnetic induction at the Royal Institution.
ppl.faraday.works.3.t: The Chemical History of a Candle
ppl.schubert.t: Composer of six hundred songs, dead at thirty-one.
ppl.pushkin.t: Poet of Eugene Onegin, killed in a duel in 1837.
ppl.hugo.t: Poet, novelist and dramatist of Les Misérables.
ppl.gogol.t: Author of Dead Souls and The Overcoat.
ppl.gogol.works.0.t: Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka
ppl.darwin.t: Published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
ppl.darwin.works.3.t: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
ppl.chopin.t: Polish composer of the piano, in Paris from 1831.
ppl.dickens.t: Novelist of Oliver Twist (1838) and Great Expectations (1861).
ppl.kierkegaard.t: Danish philosopher of anxiety and faith.
ppl.wagner.t: Composer of the Ring, with his own theatre at Bayreuth.
ppl.verdi.t: Composer of Rigoletto, Aida and Otello.
ppl.shevchenko.t: Ukrainian poet and painter, exiled by Nicholas I.
ppl.marx.t: Wrote Capital in the British Museum.
ppl.marx.works.1.t: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte
ppl.baudelaire.t: Poet of Les Fleurs du mal.
ppl.dostoevsky.t: Novelist of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.
ppl.tolstoy.t: Novelist of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.
ppl.brahms.t: Composer of four symphonies, in Vienna from 1862.
ppl.peirce.t: Logician and founder of pragmatism, born 10 September 1839 in Cambridge, Massachusetts; his How to Make Our Ideas Clear of 1878 stated the pragmatic maxim. He died in Milford, Pennsylvania, on 19 April 1914.
ppl.peirce.works.0.t: On a New List of Categories
ppl.peirce.works.1.t: Illustrations of the Logic of Science
ppl.peirce.works.2.t: How to Make Our Ideas Clear
ppl.tchaikovsky.t: Composer of Swan Lake, Eugene Onegin and the Pathétique.
ppl.nietzsche.t: Philologist at Basel, author of Thus Spoke Zarathustra.
ppl.freud.works.2.t: Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality
ppl.planck.works.0.t: On the Second Law of Mechanical Heat Theory (thesis)
ppl.planck.works.1.t: The radiation law and the quantum hypothesis
ppl.planck.works.2.t: Lectures on the Theory of Heat Radiation
ppl.husserl.t: Founder of phenomenology, born 8 April 1859 in Prossnitz in Moravia; the Logical Investigations of 1900–01 and the Ideas of 1913 set its method. He died in Freiburg on 27 April 1938.
ppl.chekhov.t: Playwright and short-story writer; died at Badenweiler in 1904.
ppl.debussy.t: Composer of Pelléas and La Mer.
ppl.marie-curie.t: Born in Warsaw; Nobel prizes in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) for her work in Paris.
ppl.marie-curie.works.0.t: Discovery of polonium and radium (with Pierre Curie)
ppl.gandhi.t: Led the Salt March in 1930; shot in Delhi on 30 January 1948.
ppl.lenin.t: Returned to Petrograd in April 1917 and led the October Revolution; died at Gorki in 1924.
ppl.russell.t: Logician and author of Principia Mathematica.
ppl.rachmaninoff.t: Pianist and composer, in exile after 1917.
ppl.thomas-mann.t: Novelist of Buddenbrooks and The Magic Mountain.
ppl.stalin.t: Led the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death in Moscow in 1953.
ppl.einstein.t: Relativity: special in 1905, general in Berlin in 1915; later at Princeton.
ppl.einstein.works.0.t: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies (special relativity)
ppl.einstein.works.1.t: Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content? (E = mc²)
ppl.stravinsky.t: Composer of The Rite of Spring for Paris in 1913.
ppl.eliot.works.0.t: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
ppl.hitler.t: Chancellor of Germany from 30 January 1933; his war and genocide killed tens of millions.
ppl.wittgenstein.t: Author of the Tractatus and the Philosophical Investigations.
ppl.pasternak.t: Poet and author of Doctor Zhivago.
ppl.bulgakov.t: Author of The Master and Margarita.
ppl.prokofiev.t: Composer of Romeo and Juliet and Peter and the Wolf.
ppl.tsvetaeva.t: Poet of the Silver Age, who took her life in 1941.
ppl.mao.t: Proclaimed the People's Republic from Tiananmen on 1 October 1949.
ppl.nabokov.t: Novelist of Lolita and Pale Fire, in exile from 1919.
ppl.popper.t: Philosopher of science, born in Vienna on 28 July 1902; the Logic of Scientific Discovery of 1934 made falsifiability the mark of science and The Open Society of 1945 the case against Plato, Hegel and Marx. He died in London on 17 September 1994.
ppl.popper.works.1.t: The Open Society and Its Enemies
ppl.shostakovich.t: Composer of fifteen symphonies, the seventh for besieged Leningrad.
ppl.arendt.t: Author of The Origins of Totalitarianism.
ppl.turing.t: Broke Enigma at Bletchley and defined the computable.
ppl.camus.t: Author of The Stranger and The Plague.
ppl.solzhenitsyn.t: Author of The Gulag Archipelago, Nobel laureate.
ppl.solzhenitsyn.works.0.t: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
ppl.mandela.t: Twenty-seven years in prison; president of South Africa from 1994 to 1999.
ppl.rawls.t: Political philosopher, born in Baltimore on 21 February 1921; A Theory of Justice of 1971 asked what principles people would choose behind a veil of ignorance. He died at home in Lexington, Massachusetts, on 24 November 2002.
ppl.foucault.t: Historian of madness, prisons and sexuality.
ppl.brodsky.t: Leningrad poet, exiled in 1972, Nobel laureate of 1987.
ppl.hawking.t: Cosmologist of black holes and A Brief History of Time.
ppl.hawking.works.1.t: The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time (with Ellis)
